title: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
summary: How a .c file becomes a program, what a pointer really stores, why arrays and strings are just bytes, how long memory lives, and how to catch the undefined behavior C will not catch for you.
outcomes: Explain the four toolchain stages and tell a compile error from a link error
Trace how &, * and pointer arithmetic read and write specific bytes in memory
Explain array decay and why a C function needs a buffer's length passed in
Choose the right storage duration and manage malloc, realloc and free without leaks
Recognize common undefined behavior and catch it with warnings, ASan and UBSan

lessons.title: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages

blocks.md:
In the prerequisite course you saw that a CPU runs machine instructions stored in memory. C is the language that sits closest to that picture: you write text, and a *toolchain* (a chain of programs: preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker) turns it into those instructions ahead of time. There is no interpreter at run time.

Why care about the stages? Because every error message comes from one of them, and knowing which one tells you what to fix. A missing semicolon, a missing header and a missing function definition fail in three different places.

The GCC manual puts it this way: compilation involves up to four stages, **preprocessing, compilation proper, assembly and linking**, always in that order. Each stage has a flag that stops right after it:

- `gcc -E main.c` stops after preprocessing and prints the expanded C.
- `gcc -S main.c` stops after compiling and writes assembly to `main.s`.
- `gcc -c main.c` stops after assembling and writes the object file `main.o`.
- `gcc main.o area.o -o app` runs only the link step.

Clang accepts the same flags. The C standard describes the same idea as eight abstract *translation phases*: phase 4 runs the preprocessor and phase 8 resolves external references and links in library code.

blocks.caption: Three files. The header only promises that area exists; area.c actually provides it.

blocks.title: One source file's trip from main.c to an executable

scenes.caption: Inputs: main.c, which you wrote, and square.h, a header it includes. Nothing here is machine code yet; it is all text.

Stage 1, preprocessing: #include pastes square.h into the text and macros such as SQUARE(3) are expanded. The result, main.i, is plain C with no directives left, only # line markers recording which file each line came from.
Stage 2, compilation proper: the compiler type-checks main.i and translates it into assembly for one CPU (main.s). Syntax and type errors stop the build here.
Stage 3, assembly: main.s becomes main.o, an object file with machine code plus a symbol table. It defines main but only refers to area and printf: they are undefined symbols (nm prints U).
Stage 4, linking: the linker takes main.o, area.o (compiled separately from area.c) and the C library, matches each undefined symbol to a definition, and writes the executable.
Forget area.o on the command line and stages 1 to 3 still succeed. Only the linker notices that nobody defines area: "undefined reference to area" is a link error, not a compile error.

blocks.md:
After `gcc -E main.c`, the call in `main` reads `printf("%d %d\n", ((3) * (3)), area(2, 5));`. The preprocessor is pure text substitution: it knows nothing about types or values. The header's declaration of `area` is pasted in too, which is all the compiler needs to type-check the call.

Each `.c` file is compiled on its own as a *translation unit*: the source file plus everything it includes. When compiling `main.c`, the compiler never sees `area.c`. It emits a call to a symbol named `area` and leaves the address blank for the linker to fill in.

blocks.code:
gcc -c main.c          # makes main.o
gcc -c area.c          # makes area.o
nm main.o
#                  U area      (used here, defined elsewhere)
# 0000000000000000 T main      (defined here; T means code)
#                  U printf
gcc main.o -o app      # link error: area is never defined
gcc main.o area.o -o app && ./app
# 9 10
blocks.caption: nm lists an object file's symbols. Checked with clang on macOS, which also prefixes each name with an underscore; GNU ld on Linux reports the failure as "undefined reference to `area'".

blocks.prompt: Suppose the header instead said `#define SQUARE(x) x * x` (no parentheses). What does `SQUARE(1 + 2)` evaluate to?
blocks.reveal: **5**, not 9. The preprocessor pastes the argument text unchanged, so the compiler sees `1 + 2 * 1 + 2`, and multiplication binds tighter than addition. That is why macro bodies wrap every parameter, and the whole expression, in parentheses, and why many C programmers prefer small `static inline` functions, which evaluate their argument once with normal C rules.

blocks.md: A header declaring a function is not the same as the function existing. `#include` only pastes a promise into your file. If the definition lives in `area.c` (or a library), it must also reach the linker, or the build fails at link time with an undefined symbol error even though every file compiled cleanly.
Compile each `.c` file separately into a `.o`, then link them. The preprocessor pastes text, the compiler checks one translation unit at a time, and the linker joins units together by symbol name.

blocks.question: Your build prints "undefined reference to `area'". `main.c` already has `#include "square.h"`, which declares `area`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add another #include "square.h" to area.c
Pass area.c (or area.o) to the link command
Compile main.c with -O2 so the call is inlined
Add the -E flag so the macro is expanded
blocks.explain: This message comes from the linker: main.o refers to the symbol area but no object file or library on the command line defines it. Headers only declare. The fix is to give the linker the definition, for example `gcc main.c area.c -o app`.

blocks.question: What does `gcc -c main.c` produce?
options: An executable called a.out
Preprocessed C text on standard output
An object file main.o with unresolved references to area and printf
Assembly code in main.s
blocks.explain: -c stops after the assembler: the result is an object file. It is not runnable because the linker has not yet resolved area and printf. -E gives preprocessed text and -S gives assembly.

lessons.title: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores

blocks.md:
Recall from the prerequisite: memory is a huge array of bytes, each with a numeric address. In C, every variable names an *object*, which the standard defines as a region of data storage. The object's address is the address of its first byte, and its *type* says how many bytes it spans and how to read them.

Two operators connect the two views. `&x` gives the address of the object `x`. If `p` holds an address, `*p` (dereference) means 'the object at that address'.

Sizes are set by the platform, not by the language. Measured with `sizeof` on a 64-bit Mac (clang, arm64), which matches 64-bit Linux on x86-64: `char` 1 byte, `int` 4, `long` 8, `double` 8, and **every object pointer 8**, whatever it points to. A pointer's *type* (`int *`, `char *`) does not change its size. It tells the compiler how many bytes `*p` reads or writes and how to interpret them.

blocks.title: Bytes in memory: an int, then a pointer to it

scenes.caption: Simplified, made-up addresses. Memory is a long run of numbered bytes. Before anything runs, the bytes the compiler set aside for x and p hold leftover garbage.
int x = 42; writes 4 bytes starting at 0x1000. 42 is 0x2a. On little-endian CPUs (x86-64, and the arm64 Mac used to check these numbers) the lowest byte is stored first.
int *p = &x; stores the address 0x1000 in p's own 8 bytes at 0x1008. A pointer is just an object whose value is an address. Here &x means 'the address of x'.
*p = 7; follows p: read the address 0x1000 out of p, then write an int there. Because p has type int *, exactly 4 bytes are written. x is now 7 although the statement never named x.

blocks.md: Why do pointers exist at all? Because C passes every function argument **by value**: the function gets a copy. A function that receives an `int` can change its copy but never the caller's variable. Hand it the variable's address instead, and it can reach back into the caller's memory. The classic example is `swap`.

blocks.title: swap: changing the caller's variables through pointers

scenes.caption: main creates two ints. Suppose (made-up addresses) x lives at 0x1000 and y at 0x1004.
C passes every argument by value. Here the values copied into swap are the addresses &x and &y, so a and b are new pointer variables holding 0x1000 and 0x1004.
t = *a reads the int that a points to, which is x.
*a = *b copies y's value into x, through the pointers.
*b = t finishes the swap. When swap returns, a, b and t disappear, but the writes went to main's x and y.
Back in main the values really are swapped.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite swap as `void swap(int a, int b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }` and call `swap(x, y)` with x = 1, y = 2. What does main print?
blocks.reveal: **1 2**. The function swapped its own copies, which vanished when it returned. Nothing it did could touch main's x and y because it never knew where they lived. This is the single most common reason a C function takes a pointer parameter: to modify, or avoid copying, the caller's object.

blocks.code:
int x = 5;
int *p = &x;     /* p holds x's address           */
int **pp = &p;   /* pp holds p's address          */
**pp = 9;        /* *pp is p, **pp is x: x is now 9 */

int *a, b;       /* careful: a is int *, b is plain int */
int *q = NULL;   /* null pointer: points to no object  */
blocks.caption: The * binds to each declarator, not to the type: write one declaration per line to avoid surprises.

blocks.md: A null pointer or an uninitialized pointer does not point to any object, and dereferencing it is *undefined behavior*: the C standard places no requirements on what happens. Often you get a crash (a segmentation fault on Linux), but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so do not rely on a crash to tell you.
A pointer is a variable whose value is an address. `&` takes an address, `*` follows one, and the pointer's type decides how many bytes are read or written at that address.

blocks.question: Given `int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p; **pp = 9;`, what is the value of x?
options: 5, because only pp was assigned
It is undefined behavior
The address of p
blocks.explain: *pp is the object pp points to, which is p. **pp follows p one more step, reaching x. Assigning 9 through it writes into x. All of this is well defined because every pointer points to a live object of the right type.

blocks.question: On a 64-bit Linux or macOS machine, `char *c;` What are `sizeof c` and `sizeof *c`?
options: 1 and 1
8 and 8
8 and 1
1 and 8
blocks.explain: c is a pointer, and object pointers are 8 bytes on these platforms. *c is the char it would point to, which is 1 byte by definition. sizeof only looks at types, so it is fine to apply it even though c is uninitialized.

blocks.md: An array in C is a fixed number of elements of one type stored *contiguously*: element i starts exactly i element-sizes after element 0. That layout is what makes indexing cheap, one multiply and one add, and it is also why C can hand you an array as a bare pointer.

Two rules from the standard explain almost everything:

1. **Decay.** An expression of array type is converted to a pointer to its first element, *except* when it is the operand of `sizeof`, the operand of unary `&`, or a string literal used to initialize an array.
2. **Subscripting is pointer arithmetic.** `E1[E2]` is defined to be identical to `*((E1) + (E2))`, and adding n to a pointer moves it n *elements*, not n bytes.

blocks.caption: For int *p with 4-byte ints: p + 2 is 8 bytes past p. For char * it would be 2 bytes.

blocks.title: int a[5]: pointer arithmetic counts elements, not bytes

scenes.caption: int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; five ints back to back, 4 bytes each (made-up start address 0x1000). Slot 5 is not part of the array; it is shown only to mark where the array ends.
int *q = a; In most expressions an array name converts ('decays') to a pointer to its first element, so q holds 0x1000, the address of a[0].
q + 2 is 0x1008, not 0x1002: adding n to an int * moves n ints, that is n x 4 bytes. So *(q + 2) is 30, and a[2] is literally defined as *(a + 2).
int *r = &a[3]; r - q is 3, the number of elements between them, not 12 bytes. The type of that difference is ptrdiff_t.
a + 5 points one past the last element (0x1014). The standard allows you to form and compare this pointer, which is how loops like it != a + 5 stop. You may not dereference it.
Reading a[5] does dereference it: undefined behavior. Nothing checks the bound at run time; the CPU just reads whatever bytes sit at 0x1014, which belong to some other object or to nothing.

blocks.prompt: main declares `int a[5];` and prints `sizeof a`, then passes a to `void f(int a[])`, which also prints `sizeof a`. What are the two numbers on a 64-bit machine?
blocks.reveal: **20 and 8.** In main, a is a real array of five 4-byte ints. A parameter written `int a[]` is adjusted to `int *a`, so inside f, `sizeof a` is the size of a pointer. The array's length did not travel with it. Clang even warns: *sizeof on array function parameter will return size of 'int *' instead of 'int[]'*. That is why C APIs pass a length next to every buffer, like `f(a, 5)`.

blocks.md:
A *string* in C is not a separate type. It is an array of `char` holding the characters followed by a byte with value 0 (written `'\0'`), which the compiler appends to every string literal. Functions like `strlen` and `printf("%s")` simply walk forward until they find that zero.

So `char s[] = "hi";` occupies 3 bytes: `sizeof s` is 3 while `strlen(s)` is 2. And `const char *t = "hello";` is a pointer: `sizeof t` is 8 while `strlen(t)` is 5.

blocks.title: A C string is bytes ending in 0, and nothing stops an overflow

scenes.caption: Simplified layout: suppose the compiler placed char name[4] at 0x2000 and char code[4] = "OK" right after it. code holds 'O', 'K' and the terminating zero byte that ends every C string.
strcpy(name, "hello") copies until it has copied the zero byte: 6 bytes into a 4-byte array. strcpy is never told how big name is, so it keeps writing.
Now printing code gives "o" instead of "OK": a variable the code never touched has changed. This is undefined behavior; with other layouts the same bug can corrupt a return address instead.
The fix: tell the copy how big the destination is. snprintf(name, sizeof name, "%s", "hello") writes at most 3 characters plus the zero byte, so name is "hel" and code is untouched.

blocks.md: Off by one is the classic C bug: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = 0;` writes a[n], one element past the end. The loop condition for an n-element array is `i < n`. Neither the compiler nor the CPU checks array bounds for you.

A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

blocks.question: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int *p = a + 1;` What is `p[2]`?
options: Undefined, p[2] is past the end
The address of a[3]
blocks.explain: p[2] means *(p + 2). p points to a[1], so p + 2 points to a[3], which holds 4. It stays in bounds: the last valid element is a[3].

blocks.question: A function `void clear(char *buf)` does `memset(buf, 0, sizeof buf);` and callers pass a `char buf[256]`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, sizeof buf is 256
It clears only 8 bytes, because buf is a pointer inside the function
It clears 257 bytes including the terminator
It fails to compile because arrays cannot be passed
blocks.explain: Inside clear, buf is a char *, so sizeof buf is the pointer size (8 on 64-bit platforms), not 256. The array's size is lost at the call. The fix is `void clear(char *buf, size_t n)` and `memset(buf, 0, n)`.

lessons.title: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory

blocks.md: A pointer is only useful while the object it points to exists. The C standard calls that window the object's *lifetime* and gives every object one of four *storage durations*: **static**, **thread**, **automatic** and **allocated**. Referring to an object outside its lifetime is undefined behavior, and a pointer to it becomes *indeterminate* (a dangling pointer) the moment the lifetime ends.

- **Automatic**: locals declared inside a function or block. They live from entry into the block until it ends.
- **Static**: globals and locals marked `static`. They live for the whole run and are initialized once, before the program starts.
- **Thread**: declared `_Thread_local`; one copy per thread.
- **Allocated**: memory from `malloc`, `calloc` or `realloc`. It lives until you pass it to `free`.

The standard never says 'stack' or 'heap'. On mainstream compilers, though, automatic objects live in the function's frame on the call stack, which is reused as soon as the function returns, and allocated objects come from the heap managed by the C library's allocator.

blocks.title: Returning the address of a local: a dangling pointer

scenes.caption: main calls int *make(void) { int n = 5; return &n; }. While make runs, its automatic variable n lives in make's stack frame below main's frame.
Inside make, &n is the valid address of a live int. return hands that value back, and main stores it in p.
make has returned, so n's lifetime is over. The standard says p's value becomes indeterminate. The bytes are still there, but they now belong to whatever runs next.

main calls another function, which reuses the same stack space for its own locals. Reading *p now may give 5, 99 or anything: undefined behavior. Clang and GCC both warn about returning a local's address.
One fix: allocate with malloc. Allocated storage lives until free is called, no matter which function returns, so the caller can safely use it and must later free it.

blocks.md:
The allocation functions are small, and their rules matter:

- `malloc(n)` returns a pointer to n bytes with indeterminate contents, or a null pointer on failure. Always check.
- `calloc(count, size)` does the same but sets every byte to zero.
- `realloc(p, n)` returns a block of n bytes holding the old contents (up to the smaller size). It may move the data. `realloc(NULL, n)` behaves like `malloc(n)`. If it fails it returns NULL and **the old block is left untouched**.
- `free(p)` releases a block. `free(NULL)` does nothing; freeing the same block twice, or a pointer that malloc never returned, is undefined behavior.

blocks.caption: A growable int array, the building block of every dynamic list in C. It prints len=5 cap=8 last=50; the figure below follows its heap.

blocks.title: A growable array on the heap: realloc may move the block

scenes.caption: Simplified heap, one cell per int, with two cells (2 and 7) used by other allocations. i = 1: v is NULL and cap is 0, so realloc(NULL, 2 ints) acts like malloc. Push 10.
i = 2: len 1 is less than cap 2, so 20 goes into the existing block with no allocation.

i = 3: len equals cap, so cap doubles to 4. The block cannot grow in place (cell 2 is taken), so realloc allocates elsewhere, copies 10 and 20, frees the old block and returns the new address. Push 30.
i = 4: 40 fits. len 4, cap 4.
i = 5: full again, cap doubles to 8 and the data moves a second time. Any other pointer still holding the old address would now dangle. Final state: len 5, cap 8, three allocations in total.
free(v) returns the block. v still holds the old address, so using it now is a use after free. Setting v = NULL afterwards makes an accidental second free(v) harmless, since free(NULL) does nothing.

blocks.prompt: Many people write `v = realloc(v, ncap * sizeof *v);` in one line instead of using the temporary nv. What goes wrong when realloc fails?
blocks.reveal: realloc returns NULL but **does not free the old block**. Assigning straight to v overwrites the only pointer to that block, so it can never be freed: a memory leak, plus v is now NULL and the next `v[len++]` dereferences a null pointer. Keeping the result in a temporary lets you still free (or keep using) the old data.

blocks.md: Every malloc needs exactly one matching free, on every path out of the function. Missing it leaks memory; doing it twice, or touching the block afterwards, is undefined behavior that can corrupt the allocator's own bookkeeping.
Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

blocks.question: Which of these functions returns a pointer that the caller can safely use after the function returns?
options: int *f(void) { int n = 1; return &n; }
int *g(void) { int a[3] = {0}; return a; }
int *h(void) { int *p = malloc(sizeof *p); if (p) *p = 1; return p; }
All three, because the bytes are still in memory
blocks.explain: f and g return the address of automatic objects (g's array decays to a pointer to a[0]), whose lifetime ends at return. h returns allocated storage, which lives until free, so the caller may use it and is responsible for freeing it.

blocks.question: After `free(p);` the program later runs `free(p);` again. What does the C standard say happens?
options: The second call does nothing, like free(NULL)
The behavior is undefined
free returns an error code
The memory is freed twice, which is harmless
blocks.explain: free on a block that has already been deallocated is explicitly undefined behavior. Only a null pointer is a guaranteed no-op, which is why some code writes `free(p); p = NULL;`.

lessons.title: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it

blocks.md: Every bug in this course so far had the same label: **undefined behavior** (UB). The standard defines it as behavior, on use of an erroneous construct or erroneous data, for which it imposes *no requirements*. The note lists the range: ignoring the situation with unpredictable results, behaving in some documented way, or stopping with a diagnostic. 'It crashed' and 'it printed the right answer' are both allowed outcomes.

blocks.prompt: The program below writes one int past a 16-byte malloc'd block (`i <= 4` instead of `i < 4`). Compiled normally with `clang -Wall -Wextra` and run, what do you expect to see?
blocks.reveal: **Nothing at all.** On the machine used to check this course it compiled without a single warning, ran, and exited with status 0. The extra 4 bytes landed in memory the program did not own, and nothing noticed. That is the danger of UB: the program can look correct in every test you run and fail later, elsewhere, or only on another compiler or optimization level.

blocks.title: An off-by-one write, without and with AddressSanitizer

scenes.caption: malloc returns 16 bytes: room for 4 ints, a[0] to a[3].
The loop condition is i <= 4, so it runs 5 times. The first four writes are fine.
i = 4 writes a[4]: 4 bytes just past the end of the block. Undefined behavior.
Built with plain clang -Wall -Wextra: no warning, no crash, exit status 0. The bug is silently there; it may corrupt allocator metadata or another object later.
Built with -g -fsanitize=address: the program stops at the first bad write, names the bug, the exact line, and where the block came from. (Real output, trimmed.)
scenes.output:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 4 ... in main oob.c:7
... is located 0 bytes after 16-byte region
allocated by thread T0 here:
  ... in malloc
  ... in main oob.c:4

blocks.md: UB is not just 'whatever the hardware does'. Because correct programs never contain UB, optimizers are allowed to assume it never happens and reason from that. cppreference's example: `int foo(int x) { return x + 1 > x; }`. If x + 1 overflowed it would be UB, so the compiler may treat the comparison as always true. Clang at `-O2` compiles the whole function to 'return 1', so a check written this way to detect overflow silently disappears.

blocks.code:
# Development build: warnings + debug info + sanitizers
gcc -Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined main.c area.c -o app
./app            # any detected error prints a report with file:line

# Release build: optimized, no sanitizer overhead
gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 main.c area.c -o app
blocks.caption: The same flags work with clang. -g records source lines so reports and debuggers such as gdb can point at file:line.

blocks.title: Which tool catches which memory bug

scenes.caption: Five bugs from this course. All are undefined behavior, and none is guaranteed to crash.
Some bugs are visible in the source alone. Returning a local's address triggers a warning from both GCC and Clang; turn on -Wall -Wextra and treat warnings as bugs.
Out-of-bounds accesses, use after free and double free depend on run-time values. AddressSanitizer instruments every memory access; Clang's docs put its typical slowdown at 2x.
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer adds checks for non-memory UB such as signed overflow: INT_MAX + 1 reports 'signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type int'.
Sanitizers only see code paths that actually run. A clean run proves the tested inputs were fine, not the program. Use them in debug builds and tests, and ship the -O2 build without them.

blocks.md: 'It runs fine' is not evidence that C code is correct. A clean run without sanitizers says almost nothing about memory safety; even a clean sanitizer run covers only the paths your inputs exercised.

Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

blocks.question: Which of these operations has fully defined behavior in standard C?
options: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u = u + 1;
int a[5]; int y = a[5];
free(p); free(p);
blocks.explain: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the power of the bit width, so u becomes 0. Signed overflow, reading one past the end of an array, and freeing twice are all undefined behavior.

blocks.question: An ASan report says `heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4 ... in main uaf.c:7` and `freed by thread T0 here: ... in main uaf.c:6`. What is the bug?
options: Line 7 reads through a pointer whose block was freed on line 6
Line 6 frees a pointer that malloc never returned
Line 7 reads an uninitialized local variable on the stack
The program ran out of heap memory
blocks.explain: ASan reports the bad access (line 7), plus where the block was freed (line 6) and allocated. Reading 4 bytes after free is a use after free. The fix is to finish using the data before freeing it, or not to free it yet.

blocks.question: A teammate says: 'Our test suite passes under AddressSanitizer, so the parser has no buffer overflows.' What is the right response?
options: Correct, ASan proves the absence of memory errors
ASan only checks stack memory, so heap overflows could remain
ASan only reports errors on paths the tests executed; untested inputs can still overflow
ASan cannot detect overflows, only leaks
blocks.explain: ASan checks accesses that actually happen at run time, on heap, stack and globals. It does not reason about inputs you never ran. Combine it with broad tests or fuzzing (running the code on huge numbers of generated inputs) to cover more paths.
